papers.title: Forest pest prediction using a hybrid Random Forest–LSTM model
papers.authors: Jiaqi Xu, Jiaqi Zhang, Xiumei Mo, Guofei Fang, Chengdong Xu
papers.abstract: Introduction Forest pest outbreaks can substantially affect forest ecosystem stability and pose challenges to forest health monitoring and risk management. However, forest pest monitoring datasets commonly contain a high proportion of zero observations and exhibit pronounced temporal variability, which can limit the predictive performance of conventional machine learning approaches. To address these challenges, this study developed a hybrid RF-LSTM framework incorporating Zero-Inflated Poisson (ZIP) features and LSTM-derived temporal features to evaluate the effects of these feature enhancements on Random Forest (RF) model performance. Methods Multi-station daily monitoring data for Coleoptera and Lepidoptera in Rui’an City, Zhejiang Province, China, were used to evaluate the proposed framework. The ZIP model was first employed to characterize the zero inflation structure of pest occurrence data, while the LSTM network was used to extract temporal representations from sequences of meteorological, seasonal, and ZIP-derived features. papers.title: MADSCAG: A Missingness-aware Early Warning System for Village-level Rice Pest Surveillance Under Reactive Monitoring
papers.authors: Mike Yuliana, Arthur Susilo, Riyadh Hadinah Ahtar Lakadimu, Weny Mistarika Rahmawati, Hendri Darmawan
papers.source: OpenAlex / International journal of intelligent engineering and systems
papers.abstract: Rice pest patrols go where farmers report trouble, so the register measures the observer as much as the pest.A forecast fitted to it inherits that bias.Is the observation process better modelled than corrected away?MADSCAG, missingness-aware decoupled stages for capacity allocation and guidance, predicts attendance and conditional severity separately on an East Java register of 114,757 village-periods, scored once chronologically.After a gap, officers found an attack 87.1% of the time against 43.1%; attendance reaches AUC 0.789 against 0.662 for a visit-rate rule; intervals cover 90.0 to 90.5% marginally, 2.1% on the largest outbreaks; the better-ranked half of visited villages holds 64.9% of recorded severity, 30% above random.No accuracy advantage over a recurrent alternative is demonstrated.Reactive registers make the visit predictable and informative, but no decision product built on it beat simpler rules, the blindspot list included; validating missed outbreaks needs prospective sampling.

papers.title: Emerging threat of Liriomyza spp. (Agromyzidae, Diptera) in horticultural crops: Species distribution, habitat shift and its semiochemical-based management strategies
papers.authors: S Renuga, Elaiyabharathi Thiyagarajan, M Karthikeyan, Srinivasan Govindaraj, Haripriya Shanmugam
papers.abstract: The genus Liriomyza (Diptera: Agromyzidae) has recently gained a reputation as a highly invasive and damaging leafminers group causing heavy economic damage in horticultural crops globally. The rising pest status of Liriomyza species is linked to climate change, protected cultivation, agricultural intensification, globalisation and movement of infested planting material, resulting in rapid geographic spread and host range expansion. The overreliance on broad-spectrum insecticides has led to insecticide resistance, pest resurgence, imbalance of predator-prey population dynamics and environmental pollution, thus making eco-friendly control approaches imperative. Among such approaches, kairomone and herbivore-induced plant volatiles (HIPVs) based strategies appear as very promising tools for species-specific monitoring and pest management. The current review provides an overview of the recent research on Liriomyza species diversity, invasion history, biology, adaptations to new environments, as well as morphological and molecular taxonomy. papers.title: Screening and evaluation of three biological control bacterial strains against Meloidogyne incognita
papers.authors: Wenjun Chen, Yuanyuan Zhou, Mengjie Miao, Limei Li, Jianghui Yi
papers.abstract: Root-knot nematodes represent one of the most severe soil-borne pathogens, causing extensive damage to plant root systems, reducing crop yields, and resulting in substantial economic losses. Owing to the environmentally sustainable and highly effective properties, biological control methods have emerged as the primary strategy for managing root-knot nematodes. Current research on the biological control of root-knot nematodes mainly emphasizes the use of biocontrol agents such as bacteria, fungi, actinomycetes. This study isolated three new strains with high nematocidal efficacy against Meloidogyne incognita. To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive report on the biocontrol efficacy of Staphylococcus warneri (GZ5), Priestia megaterium (H14), and Bacillus zanthoxyli (L16) against root-knot nematodes. These strains displayed significant nematocidal activity against several plant-parasitic nematodes, including Meloidogyne incognita , Heterodera glycines , Bursaphelenchus xylophilus , Aphelenchoides besseyi as well as the free-living model nematode Caenorhabditis elegans . Among the three strains, GZ5 exhibited the highest control efficacy, achieving 89.27% corrected mortality

papers.authors: Naveed Hussain, Umer Hayat, Benish, Muhammad Usman, Ishfaq Karim
papers.abstract: Climate-only species distribution models (SDMs) omit the host plants phytophagous pests depend on, yet pairing separately fitted pest and host models brings assumptions of its own about score comparability and threshold transfer. We examined both issues for the mango stem borer, Batocera rufomaculata , using tuned MaxEnt models for the beetle and for two economically important hosts, Mangifera indica and Ficus carica . Of five CMIP6 GCMs screened, the climatically central BCC-CSM2-MR performed well and was used for projections under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 in the 2050s and 2070s. Focal-host suitability was the cell-wise maximum of the two host surfaces, combined post hoc with pest suitability by harmonic mean. The pest model showed high spatially structured cross-validated discrimination (mean AUC = 0.883). Niche overlap was lower with F. carica (Schoener’s D = 0.14, Warren’s I = 0.38; P > 0.05), higher with M. indica ( D = 0.28, I = 0.49; P < 0.05), and highest for the pooled-host niche ( D = 0.39, I = 0.62; P < 0.05). papers.title: Prevention of Destructive Fishing in the Waters of Tual City: Effective Surveillance and Law Enforcement Strategies
papers.authors: Suharta ., Sigit Bintoro, Riyan Maulana, Ismi Isti Anah
papers.source: Crossref / International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Growth Evaluation
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Destructive fishing in the waters of Tual City remains a significant environmental and socio-economic issue, threatening marine biodiversity and the livelihoods of local fishermen. This study analyzes the problem using a SWOT approach, identifying strengths such as existing government regulations and rich marine resources, weaknesses including limited enforcement capacity and economic dependence on harmful fishing practices, opportunities such as growing global demand for sustainable seafood, and threats like illegal fishing and climate change. Based on the SWOT analysis, several policy recommendations are proposed, including strengthening law enforcement, promoting sustainable alternative livelihoods, enhancing education and awareness programs, expanding marine protected areas (MPAs), and creating market incentives for responsible fisheries. These strategies aim to transition Tual City towards sustainable fisheries management, balancing environmental conservation with economic development. Effective implementation of these policies will not only mitigate destructive fishing but also ensure long-term resilience for both the ecosystem and local fishing communities.</jats:p>

papers.authors: Annie E. Prescott
papers.source: OpenAlex / Digital Commons - USU (Utah State University)
papers.abstract: Wildfire is a natural part of Utah’s landscapes, but as wildfires become more extreme and communities continue to expand into wildland areas, it is increasingly important to understand how wildfires behave and how their negative effects can be mitigated. One way to reduce wildfire risks and protect life, property, and ecosystem services is through fuel treatments — actions that reduce the amount and arrangement of flammable vegetation through mechanical removal, wildland fire, or other methods. Information on wildfire behavior and fuel treatments is abundant but often scattered, ecosystem-specific and difficult to access. In addition, most research in the Western U.S. has focused on conifer forests, leaving other vegetation types understudied. This research addresses these gaps by summarizing wildfire and fuel treatment information for Utah and examining how fuels treatments and wildfire affect wildlands dominated by Gambel oak and bigtooth maple. Chapter II presents a practical guide to wildfire and fuel management in Utah. Different types of activity, including industrial, constructional, heavy duty ones, etc., affect the health of workers during their activities. In this study, the Multi-Objective Decision-Making (MODM) method was combined with fuzzy TOPSIS to investigate and optimize the air pollution risk affecting the health and safety of construction workers of Lar City, Fars Province, Iran. Methods: The comparison matrices (binary) and the Phillips–Perron test of different criteria and sub-criteria of health risk, including safety view, safety efficiency, understanding the risk, and risk investigation, were assessed to find the most influential factors for the optimization of the health risk of the workers. Results: Accordingly, the results indicated that “understanding the risk” followed by “safety efficiency” affected the health risk of the construction workers the most. Results: The results showed that the mean concentrations of all toxic elements except arsenic had a higher value than the background values in the world. The Top Enrichment Factor (TEF) of toxic elements of nickel, chromium, lead, and copper was higher than other elements. papers.title: Utilizing the invasive fruitwood Pyrus calleryana as substrate for mushroom cultivation, an experimental study in practical sustainability
papers.authors: Matthew D Helton
papers.source: OpenAlex / UTC Scholar (University of Tennessee at Chattanooga)
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the feasibility of using woodchips from the invasive Pyrus calleryana (Callery pear) as substrate for mushroom cultivation. Pleurotus ostreatus, Hericium erinaceus, and Ganoderma lucidum were grown on a pear wood substrate and on a conventional oak substrate to compare, yield, sensory attributes, and metabolite production. P. ostreatus showed no significant differences in yield or biological efficiency (p > 0.05), only sweetness (p = 0.022) differed significantly. H. erinaceus yield and efficiency were similar (p > 0.05), with greater second-flush yields in oak controls (p = 0.034) but no sensory differences (p > 0.05). G. lucidum performance was comparable across treatments (p > 0.05), yet triterpenoid content was reduced in pear substrates (p = 0.031). Results indicate P. calleryana biomass can sustain edible mushroom production without affecting yield or quality, while substrate composition influences bioactive metabolite synthesis, supporting invasive biomass valorization as a sustainable management strategy.

papers.title: Enhancing Rural and Indigenous Pediatric Dermatology: A Scoping Review and Practical Algorithm for Primary Care
papers.authors: Kaitlyn Ramsay, Samiha T. Mohsen, Victoria Young, Wingfield Rehmus, Rachel Asiniwasis
papers.abstract: Children living in rural and remote Canadian communities, including many First Nations, Inuit, and Métis communities, face substantial barriers to timely dermatologic care. We conducted a scoping review of common pediatric skin conditions in these settings and used the findings, supplemented by established clinical guidance and expert input, to develop a practical diagnostic and management algorithm for front-line clinicians. The review focuses on inflammatory, infectious, and environmental conditions commonly encountered in primary care and highlights contextual factors that may influence presentation, treatment, and outcomes, including geographic isolation, limited specialist access, crowded housing, water insecurity, and extreme weather exposure. The proposed algorithm is intended to support initial assessment, treatment, and referral while identifying persistent evidence gaps and the need for culturally safe, community-informed models of care.

Frostbite: diagnosis, treatment, prognosis, and future directions
papers.authors: Noor Obaidi, Olivia A Agee, Irene Yau, Robert Moritz, Kristo Nuutila
papers.abstract: From cold-weather training to deployments in high altitude and arctic conditions, frostbite injury and its sequelae remain a serious concern in military operations. Frostbite harms tissue in two distinct ways. The first involves ice crystal formation within tissue, resulting in mechanical damage and ischemia. The second occurs secondary to the inflammatory and prothrombotic state caused by reperfusion from rewarming frozen tissue. Frostbite injuries can be classified in a number of ways, but no perfect system exists. Initial work-up and diagnosis are primarily clinical. However, in equipped treatment facilities, advanced imaging modalities such as technetium- 99 m ( 99 mTc) bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance angiography, single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography (SPECT/CT), and more can play a role in diagnosis and treatment. In resource-constrained environments, such as the deployed setting, management should involve an algorithmic approach. After concurrent hypothermia and/or trauma have been evaluated for and treated, active rewarming should take place so long as there is no risk of refreezing. papers.source: OpenAlex / Advances in Social Sciences Research Journal
papers.abstract: Ensuring the security of Mongolia’s state borders and the effective organization of border protection activities are influenced by various social, economic, political, and epidemiological factors. Among these, the emergence and spread of particularly dangerous infectious diseases affecting humans, livestock, and wildlife constitute a significant challenge, particularly in the context of Mongolia’s traditional nomadic livestock husbandry and distinctive natural and climatic conditions. The outbreak of such diseases may necessitate the implementation of quarantine regimes and specific restrictions at designated sections of the state border. However, violations of established restrictions, regulations, instructions, and legal requirements may occur when individuals prioritize personal interests over public safety and collective welfare. Such violations can undermine the effectiveness of disease prevention and control measures and create additional challenges for state border security. papers.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Minimally invasive coronary artery bypass grafting (MICS CABG) via left anterior thoracotomy has emerged as a less invasive alternative to conventional open sternotomy (OPEN CABG), offering potential benefits in perioperative outcomes and complication rates. Objective. The aim of this study was to compare procedural characteristics, ventilation duration, drainage volumes, and postoperative complications between MICS CABG and OPEN CABG in a single-center cohort in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Methods. This retrospective cross-sectional study included 262 patients who underwent surgical revascularization between January 2019 and June 2023. Results. MICS CABG was associated with a shorter median procedure time (2.5 vs. 3.5 hours, p<0.001) and reduced mechanical ventilation duration (11.0 vs. 14.0 hours, p<0.001). Although ICU stay was similar (3.0 days, p=0.001), total hospitalization was shorter for MICS CABG (6.0 vs. 7.0 days, p<0.001). papers.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting integrates engineering, materials science, and biology to fabricate living tissues with precise spatial control. By enabling the layer-by-layer deposition of cells and biomaterials, it overcomes many limitations of traditional scaffold-based tissue engineering and offers new opportunities for regenerative and personalized medicine. This review presents a comprehensive overview of recent advances in 3D bioprinting. It introduces a systematic, ASTM-aligned classification of key bioprinting modalities, extrusion, jetting, and vat photopolymerization, along with their respective material and biological design requirements. It also summarizes recent progress in bio-ink development and crosslinking strategies that improve print fidelity and functional tissue maturation. In addition, the review highlights applications in both systemic disease modelling and treatment (such as cardiovascular, endocrine/metabolic, and neurodegenerative disorders) and localized tissue repair (including skin, musculoskeletal, cartilage, and bone), emphasizing their relevance to civilian healthcare and military medicine. papers.title: Delay-induced coexistence, extinction and oscillations in a lizard system with asymmetric dispersal, intraguild predation and interspecific competition
papers.authors: Jiayi Lin, Chunjin Wei
papers.abstract: The predator-prey system comprising brown anoles and curly-tailed lizards provides an ecological case study for investigating population dynamics and informing conservation efforts. The paper considers a delay lizard population model that incorporates interspecific competition, intraguild predation, and the asymmetric dispersal of brown anoles. We analyse the stability of the equilibria and investigate the existence of delay-induced Hopf bifurcation. Under the influence of delay, our analysis and numerical results suggest that: (1) A longer delay slows down population renewal, and if it exceeds a critical threshold, it may induce periodic oscillations; (2) Increasing intraguild predation and interspecific competition drives brown anoles to extinction; (3) The diffusion rate shows a non-monotonic effect: low dispersal weakens population recovery, moderate dispersal promotes stability and persistence, while high dispersal leads to instability by reducing spatial heterogeneity. papers.title: Abiotic and biotic stresses affecting honey bees: A review
papers.authors: Mohammad Ilyas Motmayen
papers.source: OpenAlex / Aureviaj Journal of Natural Sciences
papers.abstract: Honey bees (Apis mellifera) are indispensable pollinators that underpin global food production and biodiversity, yet their colonies face unprecedented challenges from a complex web of environmental and anthropogenic stressors. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the major biotic and abiotic threats undermining honey bee health, emphasizing the interactive and cumulative effects that often prove more damaging than individual stressors acting alone. The ectoparasitic mite Varroa destructor, in concert with vectored viruses particularly Deformed Wing Virus (DWV) emerges as the most devastating biotic threat, forming a mutualistic symbiosis that perpetuates escalating immunosuppression and colony decline. Beyond parasites, pathogens including Nosema ceranae, bacterial diseases and fungal infections, alongside large predators such as the predatory wasps, pose significant challenges. papers.title: Pathophysiology-guided biomarkers and therapeutics for precision trauma medicine in polytrauma with musculoskeletal injuries
papers.authors: Rex Jeya Rajkumar Samdavid Thanapaul, Manoj Govindarajulu, Chetan Y. Pundkar, Peethambaran Arun
papers.abstract: Polytrauma with predominant musculoskeletal (MSK) injury, resulting from blast, blunt, and crush mechanisms, remains a leading and complex challenge in both military and civilian medicine. These injuries not only disrupt tissues structurally but also trigger systemic cascades involving immune imbalance, endothelial dysfunction, mitochondrial stress, and premature cellular senescence. Such pathological processes contribute to both immediate clinical instability and long-term complications such as fibrosis, aberrant bone formation, neuroinflammation, and chronic disability. Conventional injury assessments, which rely heavily on anatomical scoring and nonspecific blood markers, fail to capture the dynamic molecular landscape underlying these conditions. To address this critical gap, we performed a comprehensive scoping review integrating evidence from basic science, translational studies, and clinical research published between January 2000 to June 2025, with particular emphasis on recent advances. papers.title: A fine-grained multitrophic biodiversity and environmental dataset for understanding global change impacts in drylands
papers.authors: Ana Morales‐González, Walter Ralph Jubber, Daniela Abegg, Dominik M. Behr, Tharina L. Bird
papers.abstract: Abstract Drylands harbour unique biodiversity that is increasingly threatened by climatic extremes and ongoing global change. Yet, biodiversity data, particularly for terrestrial soil invertebrates, remain extremely scarce. Here, we present a fine-grained multitrophic biodiversity and environmental database from the southern Kalahari, South Africa, comprising twelve interoperable datasets collected since 2023 across a study area of 7,294 ha spanning contrasting macrohabitats and land-use types. The core dataset contains abundance records for 394 above- and below-ground invertebrate species and morphospecies, collected through monthly live trapping. Complementary datasets include invertebrate biomass, vegetation composition, camera-trap records of 39 vertebrate species, more than 5.2 million soil temperature and moisture measurements, and spatial metadata. Shared spatial and temporal identifiers enable integrated analyses across trophic levels, environmental conditions, and spatial scales. The resource provides a growing baseline for investigating species activity patterns and biodiversity responses to land use, climatic variability, and global change in dryland ecosystems.
